samples.title: Chronicle Backend
samples.tagline: Append an immutable fact and read one event source's history through a focused HTTP API.
highlights: Configure one named Chronicle event store
Use ConceptAs and EventSourceId for clear domain values and identities
Read the stored history without introducing a projection
limitations: The sample teaches the event log directly and intentionally leaves out projections and a frontend.
Its tests specify the Chronicle-facing behavior without starting external infrastructure.

samples.title: Chronicle TypeScript Client
samples.tagline: Append a fact from Node.js, let a reactor respond, and read the combined history.
highlights: Connect to Chronicle from Node.js with the @cratis/chronicle client
Append an immutable event and wait for its observers to catch up
Return a side-effect event from a reactor and read both facts back
limitations: The sample is a single console run and intentionally leaves out projections, read models, and a frontend.
It runs against the local Chronicle development container and does not include automated specs.
The published @cratis/chronicle client must match the Chronicle server's gRPC contracts; the README lists the currently verified server tag.

samples.title: Learning path
samples.tagline: Learn event sourcing step by step: append events, project a read model, serve it through Arc, react to checkout, specify behavior, protect commands, and prepare for production.
highlights: Append events to the event log and read one event source's history back
Declare a projection with model-bound attributes and read the read model it builds
Turn the same events and read model into an Arc command and query API
React to checkout with a visible side effect and a returned follow-up event
Specify decisions, command appends, projections, and reactors without a Chronicle server
Reject invalid values, protect state-dependent decisions, and require a customer role for checkout
Run production Chronicle with trusted TLS, JWT authentication, health probes, and distributed traces
limitations: Each step is a separate, self-contained project, so the domain types are repeated on purpose.
Only step 06 (changing events over time) is coming later, waiting on Chronicle event-generation support.
Steps 01–07 use development infrastructure; step 08 runs a separate production-shaped local stack. The specs run in-process without verifying a real server or HTTP transport.

Step 07 trusts unsigned identity headers only in Development. Step 08 validates JWTs but does not enforce cart ownership; its local MongoDB, Keycloak database, demo password grant, and anonymous dashboard need hardening before deployment.

samples.title: Chronicle Processing
samples.tagline: See one event stream feed a projection, reducer, and reactor without timing guesses.
highlights: Use ConceptAs values and an EventSourceId identity throughout the model
Compare a model-bound projection with a prior-state reducer
Return a deterministic follow-up event from a reactor
limitations: The endpoint uses fixed sample data so the processing styles stay in focus.
The sample is backend-only and uses local Chronicle development infrastructure.

samples.title: Chronicle Projection Styles
samples.tagline: Build one order four ways and see where event counters differ from state-derived line counts.
prerequisites: Docker and a browser only for the optional Workbench preview
highlights: Compare model-bound attributes, a fluent projection, a stream-local reducer, and a PDL declaration
Join product names into keyed order lines and update the root timestamp from child-only events
Specify duplicate adds, quantity changes, removals, and cancellation without Docker
limitations: Projection counters count add/remove events, not distinct active lines; only the reducer derives the exact count.
The stream-local reducer cannot join cross-stream product names, so those names remain null.
PDL is for server-side Workbench preview and is not covered by the in-process specs.
The specs substitute storage, observer lifecycle, event context, join-key resolution, and compliance processing.

samples.title: Idea Loom — Arc + React
samples.tagline: Build a polished command-and-query experience with generated contracts and no event sourcing.
highlights: Use ConceptAs values and validators in a model-bound Arc command
Generate TypeScript command, query, and read-model contracts
Compose React MVVM, an observable query, and a Cratis CommandDialog
limitations: The current-state store is in memory so the Arc and React boundary stays easy to see.
This sample deliberately does not use Chronicle.

samples.title: Full-stack author registration
samples.tagline: Register an author and watch the projected list update in a React screen.
highlights: Return AuthorRegistered from the RegisterAuthor command
Project AuthorRegistered into an observable Author read model
Use generated command and query proxies in a React screen
limitations: The sample uses the template's development credentials and local Chronicle/MongoDB containers; do not deploy them as-is.
It covers only author registration and listing, not a complete library application.

samples.title: Chronicle Multi-Tenancy
samples.tagline: Use Arc header tenancy to isolate the same workflow in separate Chronicle namespaces.
highlights: Resolve the tenant from Arc's standard header
Map tenant context to Chronicle namespaces
Use the same EventSourceId safely in tenant A, tenant B, and Default
limitations: The tenant header selects context but is not an authorization policy.
The sample is backend-only and uses local development infrastructure.

samples.title: Chronicle Cross-Store
samples.tagline: Connect two named event stores through a typed outbox, filtered inbox, and local translation.
highlights: Keep Orders and Fulfillment in separate event stores
Forward one narrow contract through source outbox and target inbox
Translate the contract into a target-owned event and read model
limitations: Cross-store processing is asynchronous and is not a distributed transaction.
The sample does not claim exactly-once delivery.

samples.title: Chronicle with ASP.NET Core
samples.tagline: Host the same event-processing concepts behind a small HTTP API.
highlights: Configure Chronicle through ASP.NET Core dependency injection
Register reducers, projections, reactors, and query services
Append events through minimal HTTP endpoints
limitations: The sample concentrates on backend hosting and does not include a browser frontend.
Its HTTP surface is deliberately small.

samples.title: Chronicle Operations Diagnosis
samples.tagline: Create one deterministic failed partition and find it with the CLI and Workbench.
highlights: Use typed probe identity and name values
Create one stable reactor failure
Inspect the event, observer, and failed partition without repair actions
limitations: The POST endpoint intentionally creates local fixture data.
Replay, retry, quarantine changes, redaction, and administration are outside the sample.

samples.title: Coffee counter — Arc runtime event model
samples.tagline: Open an Arc + Chronicle application's embedded event model in the browser.
highlights: Map the viewer explicitly in Development
Explore commands, events, and an orders projection
Use cratis view without starting the application or Chronicle
limitations: The board describes application structure, not live event history.
This local-only example omits validation, authentication, and lifecycle guards.

samples.title: Community kitchen — from Marten and Wolverine
samples.tagline: Generate, validate, and review an event-model starting point from original C# source.
prerequisites: VS Code or an MCP Apps-capable chat client or a browser
highlights: Generate with the critter-stack provider without starting PostgreSQL
Compare unchanged generated output with a separately reviewed model
Inspect explicit Marten writes and a Wolverine aggregate handler
limitations: Human review is required: command/event links and aggregate-handler decisions are not fully recovered.
Marten and Wolverine are projects of JasperFx Software; this sample is not affiliated with or endorsed by JasperFx.

samples.title: Model-First Library
samples.tagline: Compile one Screenplay model and run its accepted and rejected examples through Stage.
highlights: Describe concepts, a command, validation, and an event in one model
Keep accepted and rejected examples beside the behavior
Compile with Screenplay and run model specifications with Stage
limitations: The sample verifies the model and its specifications without running a live Chronicle command.
Scene UI, source generation, and Studio round trips are intentionally outside this first step.

samples.title: Generated Values Shop
samples.tagline: Declare server-owned identifiers once in a model, render them with Stage, write them by hand in Arc, and pin them in specs.
highlights: Choose a generation strategy per concept: prefixed ULID, TypeID, NanoID and random bytes
Keep generated identifiers out of the request with [GeneratedValue] Handle parameters
Use the command's received time for TypeID orders through IGeneratableInContext
Pin generated values by name, and fix the clock and tenant, in command scenarios
limitations: Stage renders time-ordered identifiers with the wall clock, not the command's received time; the hand-written project shows the context form.
Stage refuses unique constraints on generated values, so the short invite code carries a collision warning instead of a uniqueness check.
Screenplay cannot generate secrets yet; the API key is modeled as random bytes and marked [NotAudited] in the hand-written code.
A freshness guard for hand-written generated identifiers and Studio editing are not part of this sample yet.

samples.title: Library
samples.tagline: Tour a larger Cratis application with separate lending and membership experiences.
highlights: Organize behavior as cohesive vertical slices
Generate TypeScript contracts from backend commands and queries
Compose separate lending and membership applications for local development
limitations: The MongoDB profile is the current reference path for the demonstrated read models.
Some domain flows are backend examples and are not yet represented by a dedicated screen.
